propositions.text: Applicant was born in El Salvador in 1983, entered Canada in 2004, refugee claim rejected, PRRA refused, married Mr. Prado, then removed to El Salvador.
propositions.quote: Jose Renne Menjivar Melgar, the applicant, was born in El Salvador in December 1983. He entered Canada in January 2004 and made a claim for refugee protection. The claim was rejected in September 2004. The applicant then submitted an application for a pre-removal risk assessment (“PRRA”). On May 11, 2005, he was notified that the PRRA application had been refused. Three days later, the applicant married Jose Prado in Toronto. Two weeks after the wedding, the applicant was removed from Canada to El Salvador.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant's background: born in El Salvador, came to Canada, refugee claim and PRRA refused, married Mr. Prado, then removed to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Mr. Prado sponsored applicant for permanent residence despite concerns about marriage of convenience; applicant returned to Canada and lived with Mr. Prado.
propositions.quote: In December 2005, Mr. Prado sponsored the applicant for permanent residence in Canada. Despite some concerns arising from a tip received by Citizenship and Immigration Canada that the marriage was one of convenience, the sponsorship application was ultimately successful. In October 2007, the applicant returned to Canada and was granted permanent resident status. According to the applicant, he and Mr. Prado lived together in Toronto.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Prado sponsored the applicant despite concerns, and the applicant returned to Canada and lived with Mr. Prado.

propositions.text: Mr. Prado was a notable figure in Toronto's Hispanic community despite losing both arms in Colombia.
propositions.quote: Mr. Prado was a person of some renown in Toronto’s Hispanic community because, despite having lost both his arms in an industrial accident in his native Colombia, he was very active in the community and at a local evangelical church. He had a program on a community radio station and was an inspirational figure for many.

paragraphs.summary: The court describes Mr. Prado as a notable and active figure in Toronto's Hispanic community despite his disability.

propositions.text: Mr. Prado was charged with heroin importation in 2008; applicant and Mr. Prado divorced in 2009; applicant ended relationship due to Mr. Prado's lifestyle and drug involvement.
propositions.quote: In February 2008, Mr. Prado was charged with importing 800 grams of heroin when he returned to Canada from a trip to Colombia. He and the applicant were divorced in October 2009. The divorce application filed by Mr. Prado states that the two had separated on June 1, 2008. According to the applicant, he ended the relationship because of Mr. Prado’s lifestyle, including the latter’s involvement with drugs.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Mr. Prado was charged with drug importation, divorced the applicant, who ended the relationship due to Mr. Prado's lifestyle.

propositions.text: Applicant married Ada Maria Ayala de Menjivar in 2009; they had a longstanding friendship that became romantic; applicant's first romantic attraction to a woman.
propositions.quote: In December 2009, the applicant married Ada Maria Ayala de Menjivar (nee Ada Maria Ayala Angel) in El Salvador. The two had known each other since childhood but a deeper friendship developed after the applicant returned to El Salvador in 2005 and continued after he returned to Canada in 2007. Eventually, it became a romantic relationship. As will be seen below, when this happened was a live issue in this case. According to the applicant, Ms. Ayala de Menjivar was the first woman he had been attracted to romantically. Until then, all his romantic attractions had been to men.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant married Ada Maria Ayala de Menjivar, their friendship became romantic, and she was his first romantic female attraction.

propositions.text: Ms. Ayala de Menjivar was granted permanent resident status in 2014 under applicant's sponsorship; their son was born in Canada in 2019.
propositions.quote: In August 2014, Ms. Ayala de Menjivar was granted permanent resident status in Canada under the applicant’s sponsorship. Their son Renne was born in Canada in May 2019.

paragraphs.summary: The court states Ms. Ayala de Menjivar became permanent resident under applicant's sponsorship and their son was born in Canada.

propositions.text: In 2015, an Immigration Officer alleged applicant's inadmissibility for misrepresentation about his marriage to Mr. Prado.
propositions.quote: In December 2015, an Immigration Officer prepared a report under subsection 44(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act, SC 2001, c 27 (“IRPA”) alleging that the applicant is inadmissible to Canada under paragraph 40(1)(a) of that Act. Specifically, the Officer alleged that the applicant had engaged in misrepresentation by failing to disclose the true nature of his marriage to Mr. Prado in his application for permanent residence – namely, that it was a marriage of convenience he had entered into for the purpose of obtaining status in Canada.

paragraphs.summary: The court states an Immigration Officer alleged the applicant was inadmissible for misrepresentation about his marriage to Mr. Prado.

propositions.text: The misrepresentation allegation was referred to the Immigration Division for a hearing held over nine sessions from 2017 to 2018.
propositions.quote: The allegation of inadmissibility on grounds of misrepresentation was referred to the Immigration Division (“ID”) of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada (“IRB”) for a hearing. This hearing took place over nine sessions between June 2017 and November 2018.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the misrepresentation allegation was heard by the Immigration Division over nine sessions.

propositions.text: ID member concluded applicant inadmissible for misrepresentation and issued exclusion order in 2019.
propositions.quote: In a decision dated February 13, 2019, the ID member concluded that the applicant is inadmissible under paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA because he had misrepresented the true nature of his marriage with Mr. Prado. The member issued an exclusion order against the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The Immigration Division found the applicant inadmissible for misrepresentation and issued an exclusion order in 2019.

propositions.text: Applicant argued ID erred in finding misrepresentation and requested appeal allowed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.
propositions.quote: He argued that the ID had erred in concluding that he had engaged in misrepresentation. He also submitted that the IAD should allow the appeal on humanitarian and compassionate (“H&C”) grounds under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA given his establishment in Canada, the hardship he would face in El Salvador, and the best interests of his Canadian born child.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argued the ID erred on misrepresentation and requested appeal allowed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds.

propositions.text: IAD dismissed appeal, found misrepresentation, upheld removal order, and found insufficient humanitarian grounds due to seriousness and lack of remorse.
propositions.quote: Following a two day hearing, the IAD dismissed the appeal in a decision dated April 15, 2021. The IAD member found that the applicant had engaged in misrepresentation and that the removal order issued by the ID was therefore valid. The member also found that there were insufficient H&C considerations to warrant allowing the appeal under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA considering the seriousness of the applicant’s misrepresentation and his lack of remorse for his actions.

paragraphs.summary: The Immigration Appeal Division dismissed the appeal, upheld misrepresentation finding and removal order, and found insufficient humanitarian grounds.

propositions.text: Applicant applies for judicial review, contending IAD's decisions on removal order and humanitarian relief are unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The applicant now applies for judicial review of the IAD’s decision under subsection 72(1) of the IRPA. He contends that the IAD’s determinations with respect to the validity of the removal order and with respect to his request for special relief on H&C grounds are both unreasonable.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant applies for judicial review, arguing the IAD's decisions on removal order and humanitarian relief are unreasonable.

propositions.text: Court agrees removal order decision is reasonable but finds IAD's humanitarian relief assessment unreasonable and allows application for redetermination.
propositions.quote: As I will explain in the reasons that follow, I do not agree that the decision to uphold the removal order is unreasonable; however, I do agree that the IAD’s assessment of the applicant’s request for special relief on H&C grounds is unreasonable. This application must, therefore, be allowed and the matter remitted for redetermination by a different decision maker.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the removal order decision reasonable but the humanitarian relief assessment unreasonable, allowing the application and remitting for redetermination.

propositions.text: Redetermination limited to humanitarian and compassionate grounds as no errors found in removal order decision.
propositions.quote: Since the applicant has not established any reviewable errors in the decision upholding the validity of the removal order, the redetermination will be limited to the question of whether his appeal should be allowed under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The court limits redetermination to humanitarian grounds since no errors found in removal order decision.

propositions.text: Applicant argued before ID that marriage to Mr. Prado was genuine, not for status; applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar testified.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s position before the ID was that he had not engaged in misrepresentation with respect to his marriage to Mr. Prado because it was not a marriage of convenience; rather, it was genuine and had not been entered into for the purpose of obtaining status in Canada. The applicant testified at the hearing before the ID, as did Ms. Ayala de Menjivar.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argued before the Immigration Division that his marriage to Mr. Prado was genuine and testified along with Ms. Ayala de Menjivar.

propositions.text: ID member found applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar's testimony not credible and gave it little weight; documentary evidence was credible and given full weight.
propositions.quote: The ID member found that there were valid reasons to doubt the credibility and trustworthiness of the testimony of the applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar and, as a result, gave their testimony little weight. On the other hand, the member found that information in various documentary exhibits (including immigration applications and interview notes) relating to the applicant’s relationship with Mr. Prado was credible and trustworthy and would be given “full weight.”

paragraphs.summary: The Immigration Division found the applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar's testimony not credible but gave full weight to documentary evidence.

propositions.text: ID member found applicant's testimony not credible due to inconsistencies and lack of knowledge about Mr. Prado and relationship details.
propositions.quote: The ID member found that the applicant’s testimony was not credible for two main reasons: first, it was inconsistent with other accounts the applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar had provided to immigration authorities at other times about the former’s relationship with Mr. Prado; and second, the genuineness of the relationship was belied by the applicant’s lack of knowledge of Mr. Prado and of many details of their relationship as well as by Ms. Ayala de Menjivar’s account of the development of her own relationship with the applicant at a time when he was being sponsored by Mr. Prado.

paragraphs.summary: The Immigration Division found the applicant's testimony not credible due to inconsistencies and lack of knowledge about Mr. Prado and their relationship.

propositions.text: ID member concluded marriage to Mr. Prado was a façade and applicant misrepresented facts, making him inadmissible and issuing exclusion order.
propositions.quote: The ID member concluded that the applicant’s marriage to Mr. Prado was not a genuine one but, rather, “was simply a façade.” By not informing Canadian immigration authorities that the marriage was not genuine and that it had been entered into for the purpose of obtaining legal status in Canada, the applicant had “directly misrepresented and withheld material facts, as spousal sponsorship requires a genuine relationship.” Accordingly, the member found the applicant to be inadmissible under paragraph 40(1)(a) of the IRPA and issued an exclusion order.

paragraphs.summary: The Immigration Division concluded the marriage was a façade, the applicant misrepresented facts, and issued an exclusion order for inadmissibility.

propositions.text: Applicant as permanent resident can appeal exclusion order to IAD; section 67 IRPA sets grounds for allowing appeal including error, natural justice breach, or humanitarian grounds.
propositions.quote: As a permanent resident, under subsection 63(3) of the IRPA, the applicant could appeal the exclusion order made against him by the ID to the IAD. Section 67 of the IRPA provides as follows regarding that appeal: 67 (1) To allow an appeal, the Immigration Appeal Division must be satisfied that, at the time that the appeal is disposed of, 67 (1) Il est fait droit à l’appel sur preuve qu’au moment où il en est disposé : (a) the decision appealed is wrong in law or fact or mixed law and fact; a) la décision attaquée est erronée en droit, en fait ou en droit et en fait; (b) a principle of natural justice has not been observed; or b) il y a eu manquement à un principe de justice naturelle; (c) other than in the case of an appeal by the Minister, taking into account the best interests of a child directly affected by the decision, sufficient humanitarian and compassionate considerations warrant special relief in light of all the circumstances of the case. c) sauf dans le cas de l’appel du ministre, il y a — compte tenu de l’intérêt supérieur de l’enfant directement touché — des motifs d’ordre humanitaire justifiant, vu les autres circonstances de l’affaire, la prise de mesures spéciales. (2) If the Immigration Appeal Division allows the appeal, it shall set aside the original decision and substitute a determination that, in its opinion, should have been made, including the making of a removal order, or refer the matter to the appropriate decision-maker for reconsideration. (2) La décision attaquée est cassée; y est substituée celle, accompagnée, le cas échéant, d’une mesure de renvoi, qui aurait dû être rendue, ou l’affaire est renvoyée devant l’instance compétente.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains the legal framework for appealing an exclusion order to the IAD under section 67 of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant argued ID erred on misrepresentation and requested appeal allowed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under IRPA.
propositions.quote: The applicant argued under paragraph 67(1)(a) of the IRPA that the ID had erred in concluding that he had engaged in misrepresentation. He maintained his position that the marriage to Mr. Prado was genuine and had not been entered into for the purpose of obtaining status in Canada. The applicant also argued that the appeal should be allowed on the basis of H&C considerations under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argued the ID erred on misrepresentation and requested appeal allowed on humanitarian and compassionate grounds under IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar testified again before the IAD and applicant filed documentary evidence on establishment, hardship, and child's best interests.
propositions.quote: Both the applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar testified again at the hearing before the IAD. The applicant also filed a substantial amount of documentary evidence to demonstrate his establishment in Canada and to support his submissions concerning the hardship he would experience in El Salvador and the best interests of his child.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker reports that the applicant and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar testified again before the IAD and the applicant filed documentary evidence on establishment, hardship, and child's best interests.

propositions.text: ID member found significant discrepancies raising serious credibility concerns about the applicant.
propositions.quote: The ID member had found that significant discrepancies in the evidence raised serious concerns about the applicant’s credibility.

propositions.text: IAD found applicant's evidence on appeal did little to clear credibility issues identified by ID.
propositions.quote: The IAD member found that the applicant’s evidence on appeal did little to clear up the credibility issues identified by the ID.

propositions.text: Material inconsistencies remained between applicant's testimony and other accounts of relationship with Mr. Prado.
propositions.quote: There remained material inconsistencies between the applicant’s testimony and other accounts of his relationship with Mr. Prado.

propositions.text: Applicant lacked knowledge of details about Mr. Prado and their relationship expected if genuine marriage.
propositions.quote: the applicant continued to lack knowledge of details about Mr. Prado and about their relationship that it would be reasonable to expect him to know if they had been in a genuine marriage.

propositions.text: Aspects of applicant's account of relationship with Mr. Prado did not make sense.
propositions.quote: The member also found that aspects of the applicant’s account of his relationship with Mr. Prado simply did not make sense.

propositions.text: Applicant produced no evidence to corroborate claim of living together as married couple.
propositions.quote: Further, the applicant had not produced any evidence to corroborate his claim that he and Mr. Prado had lived together as a married couple.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found serious credibility issues, inconsistencies, lack of knowledge, and no corroboration about the applicant's relationship with Mr. Prado.

propositions.text: Applicant may have had romantic relationship and cohabited with Mr. Prado around 2004-2005 but insufficient evidence to find marriage.
propositions.quote: I am willing to believe that at some point, perhaps in 2004 to 2005, the Appellant may have been in a romantic relationship with Mr. Prado and they may have resided together for a period.

propositions.text: Applicant failed to give consistent evidence on memorable marriage events like proposal, wedding attendees, celebration place, separation date.
propositions.quote: The Appellant has been unable to give consistent evidence regarding what should be memorable events surrounding a marriage: the place where a proposal was made, the attendees at the wedding itself, the place of any celebration following and the date of separation.

propositions.text: More likely than not, applicant married primarily to obtain status and privilege in Canada while under deportation order.
propositions.quote: I find it more likely than not that the Appellant, who was under a deportation order at this time and whose Pre-Removal Risk Assessment application had been refused, entered into this marriage primarily to obtain status and privilege in Canada.

propositions.text: Removal order issued by ID is valid.
propositions.quote: The removal order issued by the ID is therefore valid.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found insufficient evidence of marriage, inconsistent evidence, and concluded the marriage was for status; removal order is valid.

propositions.text: IAD considered whether special relief under paragraph 67(1)(c) IRPA was warranted considering all circumstances including child's best interests.
propositions.quote: The IAD member next considered whether, having regard to all the circumstances, including the best interests of the applicant’s child, the appeal should be allowed under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA because special relief from the requirement to leave Canada was warranted.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker considered if special relief under IRPA paragraph 67(1)(c) was warranted including child's best interests.

propositions.text: Ribic factors guide determinations under paragraph 67(1)(c) in misrepresentation cases, modified slightly per Wang v Canada.
propositions.quote: Citing Wang v Canada (Minister of Citizenship and Immigration), 2005 FC 1059 at para 11, the member began by noting that, in a misrepresentation case, the Ribic factors that guide determinations under paragraph 67(1)(c) ... are modified slightly.

propositions.text: Ribic factors include seriousness of misrepresentation, remorse, establishment, family impact, child's best interests, support, and hardship.
propositions.quote: In summary, they are the following: (a) the seriousness of the misrepresentation and the circumstances surrounding it; (b) the remorsefulness of the appellant; (c) the length of time spent in Canada and the appellant’s establishment here; (d) family members in Canada, and the impact of removal on them; (e) the best interests of any child directly affected; (f) the family and community support available to the appellant; and (g) the degree of hardship caused by removal, including conditions in the likely country of removal.

propositions.text: List of factors is not exhaustive but no additional factors considered in this case.
propositions.quote: The IAD member noted that this is not an exhaustive list of potentially relevant factors (although he did not consider any additional factors in this case).

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker explained the modified Ribic factors guiding special relief decisions and noted no additional factors were considered.

propositions.text: Decision under paragraph 67(1)(c) is discretionary, weighing factors consistent with IRPA objectives including immigration system integrity.
propositions.quote: The IAD member also noted that a decision under paragraph 67(1)(c) is an exercise of discretion in which the weight of the relevant factors must be determined in the circumstances of the case at hand. This discretion must be exercised consistently with the objectives of the IRPA, which include “maintaining the integrity of the immigration system in the face of misrepresentations made by potential immigrants.”

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker noted paragraph 67(1)(c) decisions are discretionary and must align with IRPA objectives including system integrity.

propositions.text: Misrepresentation was very serious and deliberately misleading immigration authorities causing IRPA administration error.
propositions.quote: The misrepresentation is very serious. It involved the applicant deliberately misleading immigration authorities.There is no doubt that this led to an error in the administration of the IRPA.

propositions.text: Applicant showed no remorse and maintained marriage was genuine; might have admitted marriage of convenience.
propositions.quote: The applicant displayed no remorse and maintained that his marriage to Mr. Prado was genuine. The applicant “might have done better” to admit that the marriage was a marriage of convenience.

propositions.text: Applicant is well-established in Canada, owns business and home with wife, positive factor.
propositions.quote: The applicant is well-established and this is a positive factor in the appeal. The applicant arrived in Canada at the age of 20 and has spent the majority of his adult life here. He owns and operates a roofing business with four employees with the help of his wife.Together the couple own a home and have a significant amount of savings.

propositions.text: If appeal dismissed, applicant and wife deemed inadmissible; child must go with parents to El Salvador.
propositions.quote: If the appeal is dismissed, both the applicant and his wife will be deemed inadmissible.(Ms. Ayala de Menjivar would be inadmissible for misrepresentation for having been sponsored by a person who is determined to be inadmissible for misrepresentation: see IRPA, paragraph 40(1)(b).)Given that the applicant’s son is a young child, he “will have no choice but to go with his parents” to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Applicant's son is two, Canadian citizen; child's best interests slight positive factor; relocation impact limited by age.
propositions.quote: The applicant’s son is two years old and is a Canadian citizen. The best interests of this child are only a slight positive factor in the appeal. The age of the applicant’s son limits the impact of the return to El Salvador.

propositions.text: Evidence of poor education, expensive health care, gang recruitment risk in El Salvador; child's interests better served in Canada long term but speculative now.
propositions.quote: The applicant provided evidence of poor education, expensive health care, and risk of gang recruitment in El Salvador. Although the child’s interests may be better served in Canada as he gets older, this is “somewhat, but not entirely, speculative.”

propositions.text: Applicant can apply to return to Canada after five years but no guarantee of success.
propositions.quote: As well, the applicant can also apply to return to Canada after five years, although there is no guarantee that the application will be successful.

propositions.text: Applicant's son’s long-term interests probably better served in Canada but relocation now has little impact.
propositions.quote: In the long term, the interests of the applicant’s son “would probably be better served in Canada.”However, at the present time, given the child’s age, “the relocation will have little impact on his interests.”

propositions.text: Applicant and wife not close with family in El Salvador but not completely without support.
propositions.quote: The applicant is not close with his family in El Salvador.The applicant’s wife has no immediate family there apart from her mother.Nevertheless, they are not completely without support there.

propositions.text: Hardship on removal includes gang violence risk but hardship likely temporary and slight positive factor.
propositions.quote: Three areas of concern were raised in respect of the applicant and his family’s removal to El Salvador. Nonetheless, any hardship he or his family may face will be of a temporary nature and weighs only slightly as a positive factor on the appeal. Gang violence: The applicant’s testimony and country evidence establish that gang violence is a problem in El Salvador.

propositions.text: Applicant and family not recruited by gang though family paid extortion to MS-13; risk slightly increased.
propositions.quote: However, neither the applicant nor his family members have been recruited by a gang, though family members have been forced to pay extortion money to the MS-13 gang. The applicant and his family may face a slightly increased risk

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker assessed Ribic factors: serious misrepresentation, no remorse, applicant well-established, family impact, child's best interests slight, some support, hardship slight and temporary.

propositions.text: Favourable considerations do not outweigh seriousness of misrepresentation and lack of remorse; no special relief granted; appeal dismissed.
propositions.quote: Balancing all of these considerations, the IAD member concluded that the favourable considerations did not outweigh the seriousness of the misrepresentation and the applicant’s lack of remorse. Consequently, the member concluded that there were insufficient H&C considerations to warrant the granting of special relief and, thus, no basis on which to allow the appeal under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA. The IAD dismissed the appeal accordingly.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker concluded no special relief warranted and dismissed the appeal due to seriousness of misrepresentation and lack of remorse.

propositions.text: IAD’s decision is reviewed on a reasonableness standard per Khosa and Vavilov.
propositions.quote: The parties agree, as do I, that the IAD’s decision is to be reviewed on a reasonableness standard: see Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Khosa, 2009 SCC 12 at paras 57-59. That this is the appropriate standard has been reinforced by Canada (Citizenship and Immigration) v Vavilov, 2019 SCC 65 at para 10.

paragraphs.summary: The court states the IAD decision is reviewed on a reasonableness standard per Khosa and Vavilov.

propositions.text: Reasonable decision is internally coherent, rational, justified by facts and law, and entitled to deference.
propositions.quote: A reasonable decision “is one that is based on an internally coherent and rational chain of analysis and that is justified in relation to the facts and law that constrain the decision maker” (Vavilov at para 85). A decision that displays these qualities is entitled to deference from the reviewing court (ibid.).

propositions.text: Reviewing court should not reweigh evidence or interfere with factual findings except in exceptional circumstances.
propositions.quote: When applying the reasonableness standard, it is not the role of the reviewing court to reweigh or reassess the evidence considered by the decision maker or to interfere with factual findings unless there are exceptional circumstances: see Vavilov at para 125.

propositions.text: Discretionary determinations deserve particular deference but reasonableness review is robust, not rubber-stamping.
propositions.quote: Discretionary determinations such as the one at issue here are entitled to particular deference from the reviewing court. At the same time, reasonableness review is not a rubber-stamping process; it remains a robust form of review: see Vavilov at para 13.

paragraphs.summary: The court explains reasonableness review requires coherence, deference, no reweighing, and is robust but deferential.

propositions.text: Applicant must show serious shortcomings in IAD decision to set it aside as unreasonable.
propositions.quote: The onus is on the applicant to demonstrate that the IAD’s decision is unreasonable. To set aside a decision on this basis, the reviewing court must be satisfied that “there are sufficiently serious shortcomings in the decision such that it cannot be said to exhibit the requisite degree of justification, intelligibility and transparency” (Vavilov at para 100).

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant must prove serious shortcomings to set aside the IAD decision as unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant challenges reasonableness of IAD's validity of removal order and special relief denial.
propositions.quote: The applicant challenges the reasonableness of the IAD’s conclusion that the removal order is valid as well as its determination that special relief was not warranted.

propositions.text: Court not persuaded removal order validity decision is unreasonable but agrees special relief denial is unreasonable, not for all applicant reasons.
propositions.quote: As I have already stated, I am not persuaded that the decision to uphold the removal order is unreasonable. However, I do agree that the decision that special relief was not warranted is unreasonable, although not for all the reasons advanced by the applicant.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant challenges IAD decisions; court finds removal order decision reasonable but special relief denial unreasonable.

propositions.text: Applicant contends removal order decision unreasonable due to IAD misapprehending evidence materially.
propositions.quote: The applicant contends that the decision upholding the removal order is unreasonable because the IAD misapprehended the evidence in material respects.

propositions.text: Court disagrees with applicant's contention.
propositions.quote: I do not agree.

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues IAD misapprehended evidence; court disagrees.

propositions.text: Applicant submits IAD erred by confusing 2007 and 2008 events in assessing inconsistent accounts.
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the IAD’s conclusion that he had given inconsistent accounts of what happened when he returned to Canada in October 2007 is erroneous because the evidence the member relies on to demonstrate the inconsistency actually relates to events that occurred the following year.

propositions.text: Respondent agrees IAD misapprehended evidence on this point but says error is immaterial due to other unchallenged inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: The respondent agrees that the member misapprehended the evidence in this respect. However, the respondent submits that this error is immaterial because the IAD identified numerous other inconsistencies in the applicant’s accounts that have not been challenged.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant says IAD confused 2007 and 2008 events; respondent agrees but says error immaterial due to other inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Court agrees with respondent that conflation of 2007 and 2008 events is immaterial given other unchallenged inconsistencies.
propositions.quote: I agree with the respondent. The conflation of events in 2007 and 2008 could not possibly have affected the result given all the other inconsistencies in the applicant’s accounts of his marriage that the member identified and that have not been challenged on this application.

paragraphs.summary: Court agrees conflation of 2007 and 2008 events is immaterial given other inconsistencies.

propositions.text: Applicant contends IAD erred in assessing Ms. Ayala de Menjivar’s evidence about relationship development.
propositions.quote: The applicant also contends that the IAD erred in its assessment of Ms. Ayala de Menjivar’s evidence concerning the development of her relationship with the applicant.

propositions.text: Additional background is necessary to contextualize this issue.
propositions.quote: Some additional background is necessary to put this issue in context.

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues IAD erred assessing Ms. Ayala de Menjivar’s evidence; court notes background needed.

propositions.text: Interviewer notes from 2014 sponsorship interview say Ms. Ayala de Menjivar confirmed applicant was in relationship with her in October 2007 and described it as 'friends with benefits'.
propositions.quote: According to the interviewer’s notes of her sponsorship interview in March 2014 (which was conducted with the assistance of a Spanish interpreter), Ms. Ayala de Menjivar confirmed that the applicant was already in a relationship with her when he landed in Canada in October 2007. She was then asked the following question and gave the following answer: Q. And he still went to live with his spouse in Canada? A. As far as I understand when he landed in Canada his husband was waiting for him at the airport and then he went to live with him. It was nothing formal it was just a relationship of friends with benefits.

paragraphs.summary: Interviewer notes from 2014 say Ms. Ayala de Menjivar confirmed relationship with applicant in 2007 as 'friends with benefits'.

propositions.text: At ID and IAD hearings, Ms. Ayala de Menjivar and applicant said relationship in 2007 was close friendship, not romantic or sexual.
propositions.quote: At both the ID and IAD hearings, Ms. Ayala de Menjivar testified that when she stated that she and the applicant were in a relationship in October 2007, she did not mean a romantic relationship; they were just very good friends. The applicant described their relationship at that time in the same way.

propositions.text: Ms. Ayala de Menjivar said sponsorship interview questions were transcribed incorrectly; 'friends with benefits' referred to her relationship with applicant, not applicant's relationship with Mr. Prado.
propositions.quote: Ms. Ayala de Menjivar also testified that the questions and answers in the sponsorship interview had been transcribed incorrectly. She had actually been asked another question about her relationship with the applicant (which is omitted from the notes) and this is what she was responding to when she stated that the relationship was “nothing formal” and “just a relationship of friends with benefits.” Contrary to what the notes suggest, she was not referring to the applicant’s relationship with Mr. Prado.

propositions.text: Ms. Ayala de Menjivar explained 'friends with benefits' in Spanish did not imply sexual relationship; she reiterated no sexual relationship with applicant then.
propositions.quote: Further, she explained that what she meant was that her relationship with the applicant was a very close friendship. She did not say anything in Spanish that would imply that at that time it involved anything sexual (as the English phrase “friends with benefits” does). She reiterated that there was nothing sexual about her relationship with the applicant at that time.

propositions.text: Applicant confirmed no sexual relationship with Ms. Ayala de Menjivar when he returned in October 2007.
propositions.quote: The applicant also confirmed that he and Ms. Ayala de Menjivar did not yet have a sexual relationship when he returned to Canada in October 2007.

paragraphs.summary: At hearings, Ms. Ayala de Menjivar and applicant said 2007 relationship was close friendship, not sexual; interview notes were incorrect.

propositions.text: IAD found Ms. Ayala de Menjivar said applicant's relationship with Mr. Prado was 'friends with benefits' and her explanation referring to herself did not make sense.
propositions.quote: [Ms. Ayala de Menjivar] also stated [in her sponsorship interview] that the Appellant’s relationship with Mr. Prado was more of a “friends with benefits” relationship. Her explanation for this was that she was referring to the relationship between the Appellant and herself. This does not make sense as the Appellant and his wife both testified that they did not have sexual relations until after their wedding. This casts more doubt as to the nature of the Appellant’s first marriage.

paragraphs.summary: The earlier decision-maker found Ms. Ayala de Menjivar's explanation about 'friends with benefits' did not make sense and cast doubt on the marriage.

propositions.text: Court agrees IAD overlooked evidence that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar did not mean sexual relationship by 'friends with benefits' and did not say so in Spanish.
propositions.quote: I agree with the applicant that the IAD appears to have overlooked the evidence that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar did not intend to characterize her relationship with the applicant in October 2007 as a sexual one and that she did not say anything in Spanish that would have the same sexual implications as the English expression “friends with benefits.”

propositions.text: If that evidence accepted, no basis to conclude Ms. Ayala de Menjivar referred to applicant's relationship with Mr. Prado; IAD did not address or give reasons rejecting this evidence.
propositions.quote: If that evidence is accepted, there would be no basis to conclude, as the IAD did, that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar cannot have been referring to her own relationship with the applicant ... The problem, however, is that the IAD member does not addresses this evidence in the decision nor, assuming the member did reject it, does he give any reasons for doing so.

propositions.text: IAD's determination that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar's comment casts doubt on marriage lacks justification, transparency and intelligibility.
propositions.quote: Consequently, the member’s determination that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar’s comment “casts more doubt” as to the nature of the applicant’s marriage to Mr. Prado is lacking justification, transparency and intelligibility.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD overlooked evidence about 'friends with benefits' meaning and failed to justify its doubt on the marriage.

propositions.text: Gap in IAD member's reasoning raises reasonableness question but does not undermine whole decision's reasonableness
propositions.quote: this leaves a gap in the IAD member’s reasoning and calls the reasonableness of this particular determination into question, I do not agree that this undermines the reasonableness of the decision as a whole

propositions.text: Presuming sexual connotation and linking to applicant's relationship was flawed but immaterial given other evidence
propositions.quote: Even if the member should not have simply presumed that Ms. Ayala de Menjivar had used an expression in Spanish that, like the English expression “friends with benefits,” had a sexual connotation and, further, should not have concluded that she must have been referring to the applicant’s relationship with Mr. Prado

propositions.text: IAD did not attribute particular significance to this evidence, only raised more doubt about marriage genuineness
propositions.quote: there is no basis to find that the IAD attributed particular significance to this evidence; it simply raised “more doubt” about the nature of the applicant’s marriage to Mr. Prado

propositions.text: Doubts about marriage genuineness supported by much other evidence
propositions.quote: Doubts about the genuineness of the marriage are reasonably supported by a great deal of other evidence besides this

paragraphs.summary: Court finds a gap in IAD reasoning but says it does not undermine the whole decision; other evidence supports doubts about marriage genuineness.

propositions.text: IAD erred by making implausibility findings not meeting 'clearest of cases' threshold
propositions.quote: the applicant submits that the IAD member erred by making implausibility findings that do not meet the “clearest of cases” threshold established in the jurisprudence

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues IAD implausibility findings fail 'clearest of cases' standard.

propositions.text: The 'clearest of cases' principle does not apply here as member assessed internal logic, not common sense
propositions.quote: I do not agree that this principle is applicable here. The member was not assessing what could reasonably be expected to have happened in light of common sense or common experience

propositions.text: Member reasonably found internal logic wanting and drew adverse inference on credibility
propositions.quote: The member reasonably found the internal logic of the account to be wanting in material respects and on that basis (among others) drew an adverse inference about the applicant’s credibility

propositions.text: No basis to interfere with member's determination
propositions.quote: There is no basis to interfere with that determination

paragraphs.summary: Court finds 'clearest of cases' rule inapplicable; member reasonably doubted applicant's account and credibility.

propositions.text: Not persuaded IAD's decision to uphold removal order is unreasonable
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the IAD’s decision to uphold the removal order is unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: Court is not persuaded that IAD's removal order decision is unreasonable.

propositions.text: IAD erred in three respects on H&C considerations: hardship in El Salvador, lack of remorse, and child's best interests
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the IAD fell into reviewable error in three respects in its treatment of H&C considerations under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA: (1) in the assessment of the hardships the applicant would face in El Salvador; (2) in the treatment of the absence of remorse on the part of the applicant for his misconduct; and (3) in the assessment of the best interests of the applicant’s child

propositions.text: Court agrees IAD erred on remorse and child's best interests but not on hardship in El Salvador
propositions.quote: I do not agree that the IAD erred in the first respect but I do agree that it erred in the other two respects

paragraphs.summary: Applicant alleges three errors on H&C; court agrees only on remorse and child's best interests errors.

propositions.text: IAD's assessment of hardship in El Salvador is unreasonable, especially on gang risks and expectation to conceal bisexuality
propositions.quote: he submits that the IAD member assessed the risks posed by criminal gangs unreasonably. He also contends that the member unreasonably expected him to conceal his identity as a bisexual man

propositions.text: Court does not agree with applicant's submissions on hardship and gang risk
propositions.quote: I do not agree

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues IAD unreasonably assessed hardship and gang risks; court disagrees.

propositions.text: IAD accepted gang violence problem and extortion risk for deportees
propositions.quote: The IAD member accepted that gang violence is a problem in El Salvador. The member also accepted that deportees from North America could be perceived as having money and therefore can become targets for extortion

propositions.text: IAD accepted applicant and mother-in-law had been targeted for extortion
propositions.quote: The member accepted the applicant’s evidence that he had been targeted for extortion in the past, as had his mother-in-law

propositions.text: IAD found slightly increased risk of violent crime if returned to El Salvador
propositions.quote: member found that there was a “slightly increased risk” that the applicant or his family would be the victims of violent crime if they returned to El Salvador

propositions.text: IAD did not agree risk from gangs was as great as applicant contended; this is not unreasonable
propositions.quote: The member simply did not agree that the degree of risk from criminal gangs was as great as the applicant had contended. That determination is not unreasonable

propositions.text: Court's role on judicial review is not to reweigh evidence or reach different conclusion
propositions.quote: The applicant’s arguments on this application effectively ask the Court to reweigh the evidence and reach a different conclusion. This is not the Court’s proper function on judicial review

paragraphs.summary: IAD found gang violence and extortion risks but lower than applicant claimed; court finds this reasonable and not for reweighing.

propositions.text: IAD found low likelihood applicant targeted for bisexuality due to stable heterosexual marriage and no past harassment
propositions.quote: I find that the likelihood of the Appellant being targeted in El Salvador because of his bisexuality to be low for several reasons. The Appellant is in a heterosexual marriage which appears to be stable. He testified that he is satisfied with this marriage. The Appellant returned to El Salvador in February 2005 and lived with his parents for two and a half years. He was employed during part of this period. He gave no evidence that he was harassed or targeted because of his sexuality during this period. Unless he engages in a relationship with a man, I find it unlikely that the Appellant will be identified as bisexual in El Salvador and be subject to harassment or violence

paragraphs.summary: IAD found low risk of targeting for bisexuality given stable marriage and no past harassment evidence.

propositions.text: IAD's assessment of low risk of targeting for bisexuality is reasonable
propositions.quote: In my view, this is a reasonable assessment of the evidence before the IAD

propositions.text: Applicant argues IAD required him to conceal sexual identity, which would be error
propositions.quote: I do not agree with the applicant that the IAD effectively required him to conceal his sexual identity. Had it done so, this would have been a reviewable error

propositions.text: IAD accepted applicant's account that bisexuality is not overt part of life and found low risk accordingly
propositions.quote: the IAD member accepted that, on the applicant’s own account, this aspect of his sexual identity is not a significant or overt part of his life as he is now living it and on this basis found that the risk of being targeted for this reason is therefore low

propositions.text: IAD did not suggest applicant should not engage in relationship with a man; accepted low likelihood he would do so
propositions.quote: the member did not suggest that the applicant should not engage in a relationship with a man; rather, the member accepted the applicant’s evidence that suggested there was little if any likelihood that he would do so

propositions.text: This was a reasonable determination in the circumstances
propositions.quote: This was a reasonable determination in the circumstances of this case

paragraphs.summary: Court finds IAD reasonably assessed low risk of targeting for bisexuality and did not require concealment.

propositions.text: Applicant submits IAD's treatment of his lack of remorse is unreasonable
propositions.quote: The applicant submits that the IAD’s treatment of his failure to admit his wrongdoing and express remorse for it is unreasonable

propositions.text: Court agrees IAD's treatment of lack of remorse is unreasonable
propositions.quote: I agree

paragraphs.summary: Applicant argues IAD erred on lack of remorse; court agrees.

propositions.text: Sincere remorse shows acceptance of responsibility and is important mitigating circumstance for consequences
propositions.quote: A sincere expression of remorse can demonstrate a wrongdoer’s acceptance of responsibility for their misconduct and its harmful effects. This can be an important mitigating circumstance when it comes to determining what consequences should be imposed for the misconduct

paragraphs.summary: Court states sincere remorse is important mitigating factor showing responsibility acceptance.

propositions.text: R v Reeve explains remorse as mitigating at sentencing, showing insight and responsibility aiding rehabilitation
propositions.quote: A genuine expression of remorse can constitute an important mitigating consideration at the time of sentencing. When an offender demonstrates, through actions and/or words, that he or she is genuinely remorseful for his or her conduct, it can show that the offender has some insight into his or her past actions and takes responsibility for them. Taking responsibility for past conduct is an important step toward rehabilitation and gives cause for hope that the offender may be set on a path of change. The greater the genuine insight into past offending behaviour, the greater the cause for hope

paragraphs.summary: R v Reeve explains remorse as mitigating at sentencing, showing insight and responsibility aiding rehabilitation.

propositions.text: Under IRPA s 67(1)(c), remorse and rehabilitation relevant to removal relief: Chieu and Khosa cases
propositions.quote: under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA, evidence of remorse and the possibility of rehabilitation can be relevant considerations when determining whether an individual facing removal from Canada should be allowed to remain here: see Chieu v Canada ... and Khosa ...

paragraphs.summary: Remorse and rehabilitation are relevant under IRPA s 67(1)(c) for removal relief, per Chieu and Khosa.

propositions.text: Rehabilitation concerns central in criminal inadmissibility cases; Ribic factors include rehabilitation possibility
propositions.quote: Concerns about rehabilitation are often central in cases of inadmissibility based on criminality given the overarching objective of protecting public health and safety and maintaining the security of Canadian society: see IRPA, paragraph 3(1)(h). Indeed, one of the Ribic factors is the possibility of rehabilitation: see Khosa at para 7

propositions.text: In misrepresentation cases, remorse replaces rehabilitation factor but closely connected
propositions.quote: While in misrepresentation cases this factor has been modified to refer to the remorsefulness of the party for having engaged in the misrepresentation as opposed to the possibility of rehabilitation (see Wang at para 11), I see this simply as a change in emphasis given the close connection between a party’s prospects for rehabilitation and their remorsefulness

propositions.text: Whether criminality or misrepresentation, evidence that conduct unlikely to be repeated is favourable in special relief
propositions.quote: whether the issue is inadmissibility due to criminality or due to misrepresentation, evidence that the conduct that led to the finding of inadmissibility is not likely to be repeated can be a favourable consideration in a request for special relief

paragraphs.summary: Rehabilitation is key in criminal inadmissibility; remorse replaces it in misrepresentation but both relate to conduct repetition risk.

propositions.text: Remorse relevant beyond risk of repetition; supports argument removal is disproportionate
propositions.quote: remorse can also be relevant in a broader sense. Evidence of genuine contrition and acceptance of responsibility for one’s wrongdoing can add support ... to the argument that the offending party’s removal from Canada is not a proportionate step

propositions.text: Khosa requires assessing remorse weight in context of all case circumstances
propositions.quote: the weight to be given to evidence of remorse and the prospects for rehabilitation in determining whether special relief is warranted under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA must be assessed “in light of all the circumstances of the case” (at para 66)

paragraphs.summary: Remorse can support disproportionality argument for removal; Khosa requires context-based assessment.

propositions.text: Admission of wrongdoing (e.g. guilty plea) has additional benefits like saving resources and is mitigating
propositions.quote: When remorse is expressed through an admission of the wrongful conduct ... this can have additional beneficial effects ... These can also constitute important mitigating circumstances: see R v Anthony-Cook

paragraphs.summary: Admission of wrongdoing has extra mitigating benefits like saving resources, per R v Anthony-Cook.

propositions.text: Question whether absence of remorse and admission can worsen consequences
propositions.quote: But can the absence of these things make things worse?

paragraphs.summary: Court poses issue whether absence of remorse and admission can worsen consequences.

propositions.text: In criminal law, failure to plead guilty and lack of remorse cannot be aggravating factors
propositions.quote: In the criminal context, it is an error in principle to treat a failure to plead guilty and the absence of remorse as aggravating factors

propositions.text: Accused entitled to maintain innocence and not be punished for it after guilty verdict
propositions.quote: Even after a guilty verdict, “an accused is entitled to maintain his or her innocence and cannot be punished for maintaining that stance” (Reeve at para 12)

propositions.text: These criminal principles do not apply in immigration context due to no presumption of innocence
propositions.quote: these principles cannot simply be transposed into the immigration context because ... the presumption of innocence is inapplicable in the immigration context: see Chung at para 20

propositions.text: Decision maker's treatment of remorse under IRPA s 67(1)(c) must be reasonable in case circumstances
propositions.quote: the decision maker’s treatment of evidence of remorse under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA must still be reasonable in light of the particular circumstances of the case

paragraphs.summary: Criminal law bars punishing lack of remorse but immigration context differs; remorse treatment must be reasonable.

propositions.text: IAD found applicant lacked remorse because he maintained marriage was genuine
propositions.quote: the IAD member found that the applicant had not demonstrated remorse “because he maintained, throughout this appeal, that his marriage to Mr. Prado was genuine”

propositions.text: IAD said applicant should have admitted marriage was convenience and not wasted hearing time
propositions.quote: the applicant “might have done better to admit that his marriage to Mr. Prado was a marriage of convenience and not waste this Division’s time with a hearing that necessitated two sittings”

propositions.text: IAD concluded applicant's insistence and lack of remorse not a factor in his favour
propositions.quote: the applicant’s “insistence that his first marriage was genuine and his lack of remorse is not a factor in his favour”

paragraphs.summary: IAD found applicant lacked remorse because he maintained marriage genuineness and did not admit convenience.

propositions.text: IAD found misrepresentation serious, marriage was convenience, applicant showed no remorse, wasted resources
propositions.quote: I found the Appellant’s misrepresentation to be of a serious nature. The Appellant entered into what was clearly a marriage of convenience ... He continued to insist that this marriage is genuine ... Accordingly, he has shown no remorse ... He wasted the time and resources of the ID and the IAD

propositions.text: IAD concluded humanitarian and compassionate factors do not outweigh seriousness and lack of remorse
propositions.quote: The humanitarian and compassionate factors in this appeal do not outweigh the seriousness of the misrepresentation ... and his lack of remorse for so doing

paragraphs.summary: IAD found serious misrepresentation, no remorse, wasted resources, and H&C factors do not outweigh these.

propositions.text: The IAD treated the applicant's failure to admit wrongdoing and lack of remorse as aggravating factors against special relief.
propositions.quote: the member treated the applicant’s failure to admit his wrongdoing and his lack of remorse not simply as the absence of mitigating factors but, rather, as aggravating factors weighing heavily against the granting of special relief

propositions.text: It was unreasonable for the IAD to treat these factors as aggravating in this case.
propositions.quote: In my view, it was unreasonable for the IAD to do so in the particular circumstances of this case.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD unreasonably treated the applicant's failure to admit wrongdoing and lack of remorse as aggravating factors against special relief.

propositions.text: The purpose of the ID and IAD hearings was to determine the genuineness of the applicant's marriage to Mr. Prado, a key fact for misrepresentation allegations.
propositions.quote: the purpose of the hearing before the ID and, in part, the hearing before the IAD was to determine the genuineness of the applicant’s marriage to Mr. Prado

propositions.text: The underlying facts had not been previously determined by any tribunal; the Minister's claim was an unproven allegation until decided otherwise.
propositions.quote: The underlying facts had not previously been determined by any other tribunal. Unless and until the ID and the IAD determined otherwise, the Minister’s claim ... was an unproven allegation.

propositions.text: The burden of proof on the genuineness of the marriage lay with the Minister at both ID and IAD.
propositions.quote: this was an issue on which the burden of proof lay with the Minister at both the ID and the IAD

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the hearings aimed to determine marriage genuineness, the Minister's claim was unproven, and the burden of proof lay with the Minister.

propositions.text: The applicant was entitled to require the Minister to prove the marriage was not genuine and to appeal the ID's determination to the IAD.
propositions.quote: The applicant was entitled to put the Minister to the proof ... He was also entitled to appeal the ID’s determination to the IAD

propositions.text: The IAD conducts a de novo hearing on appeal from the ID.
propositions.quote: the IAD, which conducts a de novo hearing

propositions.text: It was unreasonable for the IAD to fault the applicant for exercising legal rights instead of admitting the Minister's allegation of a non-genuine marriage.
propositions.quote: It was unreasonable for the IAD member to fault the applicant for exercising these legal rights instead of simply admitting the Minister’s allegation

paragraphs.summary: The court states the applicant was entitled to require proof and appeal, and it was unreasonable to fault him for exercising these rights.

propositions.text: This case differs from cases where wrongful conduct is established in separate proceedings, such as criminal trials.
propositions.quote: The present case must be distinguished from those where the underlying wrongful conduct has already been established in a separate proceeding

propositions.text: In cases with criminal trial findings, failure to admit wrongdoing may be an aggravating factor under IRPA paragraph 67(1)(c).
propositions.quote: The Federal Court of Appeal held in Chung that ... it may be reasonable for the IAD to treat the failure to admit ... as an aggravating factor under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA

propositions.text: That reasoning does not apply here because no such prior finding exists.
propositions.quote: That is not the case here.

paragraphs.summary: The court distinguishes this case from those with prior criminal findings where failure to admit is aggravating; that does not apply here.

propositions.text: It was unreasonable and unwarranted for the IAD to conclude the applicant wasted time and resources by maintaining his marriage was genuine.
propositions.quote: it was both unreasonable and unwarranted for the IAD member to conclude that the applicant had “wasted the time and resources of the ID and the IAD in maintaining that his first marriage was genuine.”

propositions.text: Proceedings would have been shorter if the applicant admitted the marriage was not genuine, but he was entitled to require proof.
propositions.quote: No doubt, the proceedings ... would have been shorter if the applicant had simply admitted that his first marriage was not genuine. However ... the applicant was entitled to put the Minister to the proof

propositions.text: Nothing suggests the applicant acted improperly or abused the process by contesting the allegation.
propositions.quote: There is nothing to suggest that in doing so the applicant acted improperly or otherwise abused the process

paragraphs.summary: The court finds it unreasonable for the IAD to say the applicant wasted resources; he was entitled to contest and did not abuse process.

propositions.text: Determining marriage genuineness is difficult, often requiring inference from conduct and circumstances.
propositions.quote: determinations as to the genuineness of a marriage can be exceedingly difficult ... intent must be inferred from the conduct of the parties and the particular circumstances

propositions.text: Evidence supporting genuineness may be lacking even if the marriage is genuine, unlike cases with direct evidence of misrepresentation.
propositions.quote: evidence that could support the genuineness of a marriage may be lacking even though the marriage is, in fact, genuine

propositions.text: This case differs from misrepresentation cases with direct evidence, where the decision is more straightforward.
propositions.quote: These challenges distinguish cases like the present one from cases of alleged misrepresentation where the wrongful conduct can be established with direct evidence

propositions.text: It was not improper for the applicant to appeal and disagree with the Minister's allegations and ID's finding.
propositions.quote: Contrary to the view of the IAD, it was not improper for the applicant to bring that disagreement forward by way of an appeal.

paragraphs.summary: The court finds marriage genuineness is hard to prove, this case differs from direct evidence cases, and the applicant was entitled to appeal.

propositions.text: It was not unreasonable for the IAD to find the marriage was a marriage of convenience.
propositions.quote: it was not unreasonable for the IAD to conclude that the applicant’s marriage to Mr. Prado was a marriage of convenience

propositions.text: The Minister presented a strong misrepresentation case; the applicant's response had material weaknesses.
propositions.quote: the Minister had presented a strong case of misrepresentation and that the applicant’s case in response suffered from many material weaknesses

propositions.text: However, the applicant should not be faulted for maintaining a position he presumably believed to be true.
propositions.quote: he should not have faulted the applicant for maintaining a position that he presumably believed to be the truth

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD reasonably found a marriage of convenience but should not fault the applicant for maintaining his truthful belief.

propositions.text: The IAD could reasonably find the applicant showed no remorse for wrongdoing.
propositions.quote: the IAD member reasonably could have found that the applicant had not demonstrated remorse for his wrongdoing

propositions.text: It would be unreasonable to find otherwise on the record before the IAD.
propositions.quote: on the record before the IAD, it would be unreasonable for the member to have found otherwise

propositions.text: The IAD could assess special relief on absence of remorse as a neutral or negative factor.
propositions.quote: the member reasonably could have assessed the request for special relief on the basis that a factor ... was absent

propositions.text: But the IAD unreasonably held failure to admit and lack of remorse weighed heavily against special relief in this case.
propositions.quote: he held that the applicant’s failure to admit the Minister’s allegation and to show remorse were factors that weighed heavily against the request for special relief. In the particular circumstances of this case, this was an unreasonable determination

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD reasonably found no remorse but unreasonably treated failure to admit and lack of remorse as heavy negative factors.

propositions.text: The IAD took an unreasonably truncated view of his son's best interests by focusing on his young age.
propositions.quote: the applicant submits that the IAD member took an unreasonably truncated view of his son’s best interests by focusing on his son’s young age

propositions.text: The court agrees with the applicant's submission on the IAD's view of the child's best interests.
propositions.quote: I agree

paragraphs.summary: The applicant argues and the court agrees the IAD unreasonably focused on the child's young age in assessing best interests.

propositions.text: Baker requires decision makers to consider children's best interests as important, substantial, and with sensitivity in discretionary decisions.
propositions.quote: the decision maker “should consider children’s best interests as an important factor, give them substantial weight, and be alert, alive and sensitive to them.”

propositions.text: Children's best interests need not always outweigh other considerations, but minimizing them unreasonably is grounds for unreasonableness.
propositions.quote: where the interests of children are minimized ... the decision will be unreasonable

paragraphs.summary: The court cites Baker requiring children's best interests to be substantially and sensitively considered, minimizing them is unreasonable.

propositions.text: The IAD quoted these principles but did not apply them reasonably to this case's circumstances.
propositions.quote: The IAD member quotes these principles in the decision but I am not satisfied that he applied them reasonably to the particular circumstances of this case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD quoted but did not reasonably apply children's best interests principles here.

propositions.text: The IAD found the child's young age limits the impact of removal because parents would meet his needs regardless of location.
propositions.quote: The IAD member found that the age of the applicant’s son “limits the impact that a return to El Salvador would have” because ... his needs would continue to be met by his parents

propositions.text: This finding ignores likely impacts of removal on parents' ability to meet the child's needs and conditions in El Salvador.
propositions.quote: This fails to account for the likely impacts of removal from Canada on the parents’ ability to meet their son’s needs. As well, given the evidence of conditions in El Salvador

propositions.text: It was unreasonable for the IAD to find it speculative that the child's needs would be better served in Canada as he ages; more careful consideration was warranted.
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable for the IAD to find that it was “somewhat, but not entirely, speculative” that the child’s needs would be better served in Canada as he gets older. At the very least, this issue warranted more careful consideration

propositions.text: The IAD's approach wrongly suggests younger children require less consideration of best interests.
propositions.quote: The IAD’s approach also erroneously suggests that, the younger the child, the less necessary it is to consider the child’s best interests

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD unreasonably minimized removal's impact on the child and wrongly suggested younger children need less best interests consideration.

propositions.text: Due to flawed reasoning, it was unreasonable for the IAD to find the child's best interests only a slight positive factor.
propositions.quote: it was unreasonable for the IAD to find that the child’s best interests “are only a slight positive factor” in this case

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD unreasonably minimized the child's best interests as only a slight positive factor.

propositions.text: The IAD's inadmissibility determination under paragraph 40(1)(a) IRPA is not unreasonable.
propositions.quote: I am not persuaded that the IAD’s determination that the applicant is inadmissible ... is unreasonable

propositions.text: The IAD's determination under paragraph 67(1)(c) IRPA is flawed as identified and cannot withstand review.
propositions.quote: I am persuaded that the IAD’s determination under paragraph 67(1)(c) of the IRPA is flawed in the respects identified above

propositions.text: The judicial review application is allowed regarding special relief but not to reopen misrepresentation issue.
propositions.quote: the application for judicial review must be allowed in this respect. However ... there is no basis to permit the applicant to re-open that issue before the IAD

paragraphs.summary: The court finds the IAD's inadmissibility finding reasonable but its special relief determination flawed and allows judicial review on that issue only.

propositions.text: The matter is remitted to the IAD for redetermination limited to special relief entitlement, applicant bound by inadmissibility finding.
propositions.quote: the matter will be remitted for redetermination by the IAD with the direction that the applicant is bound by the IAD’s determination that he is inadmissible ... and that the redetermination is limited to the applicant’s entitlement to special relief

paragraphs.summary: The court remits the matter to the IAD for redetermination limited to special relief, applicant bound by inadmissibility finding.

propositions.text: The judicial review is allowed and remitted for redetermination by a different decision maker limited to special relief entitlement.
propositions.quote: the application for judicial review is allowed and the matter is remitted for redetermination by a different decision maker. This redetermination will be limited to the applicant’s entitlement to special relief

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review and remits the matter for redetermination limited to special relief by a different decision maker.

propositions.text: No serious questions of general importance arise for certification under paragraph 74(d) IRPA.
propositions.quote: The parties did not suggest any serious questions of general importance for certification ... I agree that none arise

propositions.text: The application for judicial review is allowed, IAD decision set aside, matter remitted for redetermination limited to special relief, applicant bound by inadmissibility finding, no question of general importance.
propositions.quote: The application for judicial review is allowed. The decision of the Immigration Appeal Division ... is set aside and the matter is remitted for redetermination ... The applicant is bound by the IAD’s determination that he is inadmissible ... No question of general importance is stated

paragraphs.summary: The court allows judicial review, sets aside IAD decision, remits matter limited to special relief, applicant bound by inadmissibility, no general importance question.
